translations.text: Beloved, it is clear to everyone that no one has written the books except by the grace of the Holy Spirit.
For the great Moses first began to describe heaven and earth, which he had never seen; but through the revelation of the Holy Spirit he described them as if he had seen them with his eyes.
And after him others also wrote books, in which they told the story of the children of Israel in order, one thing after another, up to his death.
Then were written down the sayings that they preached about the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and about his struggle in the flesh.
And after the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ these four were written,
through which the coming of the Lord is proclaimed to the generations to come, along with his dispensation in the flesh that he took from the Virgin Mary out of mercy for us,
and, after this, how they went about the whole world and preached the word of life,
and many believed them and "were baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit."
But the enemy and envier never ceased from opposing the truth. He stirred up the kings of that time, and they forced the believers to serve their idols,
and those of them who did not obey, they slew with the edge of the sword and burned with fire.
Then some men among the believers arose and began to write the lives of the holy martyrs and the manner in which their struggle came to its end,
for the glorification of the holy martyrs and as an example for those who have divine zeal to imitate.
For this same reason I too, though unworthy, wished to imitate those who came before, and I have written the life and martyrdom of the holy and blessed martyr Constantine,
who lived in our own days, in the reign of the God-fearing Empress Theodora, who ruled the kingdom of the Greeks while her son Michael was still a child.
This blessed woman purified all the land of the Greeks from the error that had existed in the days of her husband, the unbelief concerning icons.
She strengthened the struggle of the Greeks and rebuilt many towns that had been laid waste by the Hagarenes.
At that time there was a man in the land of Kartli, in the districts of Zena Sopeli, whose name was Constantine. He was called Kakhay after the name of his native land.
This man was very greatly distinguished throughout the land of Kartli. He had great wealth and many of the pleasures of this world.
His name was famous in distant lands, so much so that even kings had heard of him.
And this blessed man was adorned with both kinds of deeds, as a tree is adorned with leaves and fruit.
He had faith in our Lord Jesus Christ that did not waver and was firmer than the mountains.
The blessed man also had faith in the bishops and in all the clergy of the church, as is fitting and right.
He loved monks and had faith in them, and he was eager to serve them. And if any of the monks,
or any of the clergy at all, came to his house, he would go out to meet him with joy, bow down before him with his face to the ground, give him ample rest, and send him on his way with many gifts.
As for his hospitality to strangers and his mercy to the poor, no one is able to tell of them worthily; we will say only a little.
Who ever came to him, and where, hungry or thirsty, and he did not feed him until he was full? Or naked, and he did not gladly clothe him?
Many fled to him from distant lands, running from their creditors, and he paid off their debts with great gladness.
Where did he ever see an orphan or a widow and not quickly take care of them?
And besides all this, he took great care of the needy of his own household, for he had heard what the apostle Paul said:
"If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than the unbelievers."
The blessed man had more humility and self-abasement than anyone else, for he had heard the word of the Deliverer and Savior:
"Learn from me, for I am meek and lowly." He counted himself more sinful than anyone else and wept for his sins, and he often said:
"I have no hope of the forgiveness of sins from anywhere, except by shedding my blood for him who shed his blood for us."
His heart longed to go to the temple in Jerusalem and to worship at holy Golgotha, where our renewal was accomplished by the right hand of the Most High,
and at the life-giving Tomb clothed in light, and at holy Zion, mother of the churches, and at all the holy places where the feet of the Lord had stood.
When he reached Jerusalem, he venerated the holy places and gave great wealth to the churches,
to the poor and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Then he left Jerusalem and went round all the monasteries of the desert and the people living by the Jordan.
Through him they were granted much relief and comfort, and they sent him on his way with many prayers and blessings.
When he returned to his own land, he lived a splendid life, with much service to God.
From then on he never stopped asking eagerly about the peace of Jerusalem and the support of the poor
who lived there. Every year he sent three myriads (thirty thousand) of silver by one of his servants:
some of it for the holy places, some for the desert monasteries, and some for the poor who lived in Jerusalem.
For he had heard the commandment that the apostle Paul wrote to the Corinthians:
"Let your surplus go to the needs of those who are in Jerusalem, so that their surplus may also go to your need."
He grew old, and the blessed man reached the age of eighty-five.
At just this time of his life a great persecution arose against the Christians throughout the whole land of Kartli.
There were great battles, and many Christians who were fighting for the law of Christ were killed in them.
The blessed man was taken captive, since he was the leader and the most eminent man in all the land of Kartli and the head of his family.
They put him in fetters, took him in that state to the city of Tiflis, and locked him in prison.
But he was not afraid at all, nor was he shaken. Instead he accepted with joy what had come upon him, and he gave thanks to the Lord.
The seizure of that blessed man did not happen without God,
but through Him who governs all things and gives the human race occasions for salvation by His hidden providence.
In this too He willed that joyful peace [?], so that the good leaven of his zeal, which He had known beforehand, might be a spectacle for angels and men.
So He did not hold back his being seized beforehand [?], for He trusted in his courage, just as it was with Job and with all the saints, one after another.
When they brought the blessed man before the tyrant in Tbilisi, whose name was Bugha, the tyrant reproached him and said to him:
"Did you not know that you would escape from my hands by your flight? For there is no one among the rebels whom I have not overcome,
nor anyone who prepares to fight against us whom we do not overpower. For behold, God has given you to us this day, to be slaughtered by our hands!"
The blessed Constantine answered him and said: "I too know that God has given us into your hands, but not because He loves you,
nor because of your good deeds. It is because we did not keep His commandments, and for this reason He has cut us down by means of that nation of disobedience.
For many times the Lord also gave Israel into the hands of foreigners, whenever they did not walk in His ways.
But for me it is good that the Lord has humbled me, so that I may keep His commandments."
And he bore the oppressions of that wicked man with courage, for he remembered the word of God that says:
"Blessed are you when they persecute you and revile you, and falsely speak every evil word against you for my sake."
While the martyr of Christ was still imprisoned in Tbilisi, he wrote letters to all the hermits of the city and the superiors of the monastery, in which it was written:
"I know that you have heard what God has brought upon me because of my sins. But I entreat you, holy fathers
and true ascetics of Christ, to remember my love and my faith toward you, and to be willing to pray for me to the Lord,
not only that He may deliver me from the hands of the lawless one, but that Christ, the true God, may give me strength
against this snare set before me, which my enemy has laid, who wishes to make me stumble from the path my soul longs for."
After a few days they bound him with harsh iron fetters and sent him to the land of Babylon,
to the city called Samarra. They brought him to the king of the Ishmaelites, whose name was Jafar, son of Abraham.
When they brought the martyr of Christ before him, the king said to him: "Behold, you have been given into my hands, and I have power over you to do good or evil.
But listen to me and obey me: accept our law and renounce your error concerning Christ as God, for I see that you are a man of understanding.
How then can you confess as God a mere man, born of a woman?
